issues.subcategory: Bayes Factor contradiction between text and table
issues.description: The text states 'Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)' and 'only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42).' However, Table 4 shows BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay (strong evidence FOR the null hypothesis, not against it) and BFincl = 39110.895 for Target Type (overwhelming evidence that Target Type IS relevant). The text and table are flatly contradictory on both which factor matters and by what magnitude. A BFincl of 0.064 means the data support excluding Memory Delay from the model, yet the text claims it is the only relevant factor. Simultaneously, Target Type shows BFincl ~ 39,000 but is described as not relevant. This cannot be reconciled by rounding or presentation choices; it indicates either the wrong table was pasted, rows were mislabeled, or the analysis was reported incorrectly. This undermines the entire follow-up analysis for Experiment 2's non-illusory errors.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42, see Appendix 1 for a full model comparison and Table 4 for an overview of BFincl for each model component). Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets (2% increase, from 10 to 12%, in both real and pseudo-letter targets).

issues.subcategory: Extreme post-hoc participant exclusion creating selection bias
issues.description: In Experiment 1, 40 participants completed the study after training exclusions, but 17 (42.5%) were subsequently excluded from the main analysis because they had 10 or fewer high-confidence critical trials in at least one cell of the design. The final analysis is based on only 23 participants. Critically, the exclusion criterion is based on the dependent variable (confidence), meaning excluded participants systematically differed from included participants: excluded participants averaged 26.2% high-confidence trials vs. 53.8% for included participants. Because the entire analytical framework depends on high-confidence responses as a proxy for 'true memory illusions,' this selection procedure removes participants who tend not to respond with high confidence — precisely the population for whom the theoretical interpretation may differ. No sensitivity analyses are reported, and the implications of this non-random 42.5% exclusion for the generalizability and validity of conclusions are not discussed.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions. Included participants had on average 53.8% high confidence trials over all critical conditions (range: 36.3 – 93.2, sd: 13.9). Excluded participants had on average 26.2% high confidence trials over all conditions (range 3.6 – 47.7%, sd: 13.0).

issues.subcategory: Wrong figure number referenced in Experiment 4 results
issues.description: The Experiment 4 Results section opens with 'Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.' However, Figure 5 is explicitly labeled as belonging to Experiment 3 ('Figure 5 Experiment 3. Error rates in trials where participants indicated high confidence...'). Experiment 4's figure is labeled Figure 6 ('Figure 6 Experiment 4. Error rates in trials where participants indicated high confidence...'). This is a direct cross-referencing error that cannot be attributed to ambiguity. Readers directed to Figure 5 while reading Experiment 4 results will be interpreting results from a different experiment entirely.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA model comparison showed that the model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, Memory Delay, and all 2-way interactions (but not the 3-way interaction), had the best fit (BFm >1000

issues.subcategory: Asymmetric response display design creates unequal illusion opportunity in Experiment 1
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the probability that the mirrored counterpart of the target appeared in the response screen differed substantially between target types: for pseudo-letter targets, the pseudo-letter itself appeared in the response screen on 50% of trials, meaning the real-letter counterpart was the only option on the other 50% of pseudo-letter trials. For real-letter targets, the pseudo-letter counterpart appeared in only 16% of trials. This structural asymmetry means participants physically could not make a real-to-pseudo illusion response in 84% of real-letter target trials (since the pseudo-letter was absent from the response screen), whereas a real-letter response was always available in pseudo-letter target trials. The direct comparison of pseudo-to-real versus real-to-pseudo illusion rates — the primary evidence for Hypothesis 3 — is therefore confounded by differential response availability, not just differential world knowledge. The text acknowledges the critical trial proportions were equalized (~13% each) but the analysis is conducted across all trials, including non-critical ones, where the opportunity to respond with an illusory choice was highly unequal.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials.

issues.subcategory: Online data collection with uncontrolled timing for millisecond-precise paradigm
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via participants' personal laptops during a Zoom session, while Experiments 1–3 were laboratory-based. The paradigm critically depends on a 250ms stimulus presentation time and a 500ms short memory delay. Online JavaScript-based experiments running in a browser on heterogeneous consumer hardware introduce substantial timing variance due to monitor refresh rates (which may be 60Hz, giving 16.7ms frame intervals), operating system scheduling latency, browser rendering delays, and variable GPU performance. A 250ms stimulus at 60Hz corresponds to only 15 frames, and a single-frame error represents a 6.7% deviation. More fundamentally, the 500ms short delay is the key condition establishing that illusions occur 'within seconds' of stimulus offset — the entire premise of the paper. If this interval is unreliable online, the critical temporal claim is undermined. These timing limitations are not acknowledged as a caveat, and no validation of timing accuracy is reported (e.g., via a frame-capture test or comparison to lab-based results). The online format also precludes verification of viewing distance, screen size, and whether participants used full-screen mode, all of which affect the visual angle of stimuli.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time. Here, each participant was placed in a Zoom break-out room, and given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.subcategory: Cannot distinguish change in stored representation from biased retrieval reconstruction
issues.description: The central theoretical claim is that 'correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter' during STM storage itself. However, the experimental design cannot distinguish between two mechanistically distinct processes: (a) the stored memory trace undergoes transformation from pseudo-letter to real-letter representation during the retention interval (a true change in storage), or (b) the stored memory trace decays/degrades and at retrieval is reconstructed using top-down priors (a retrieval-time bias on a degraded but not transformed trace). Both processes would produce the same observable signature — increasing high-confidence errors over time — because in both cases a weakened trace interacts with prior knowledge to produce an incorrect report. Distinguishing these accounts would require measuring the memory trace itself (e.g., via neuroimaging or a concurrent signal-detection measure), not just the behavioral report. The temporal increase in errors is claimed as proof of a 'memory illusion' arising during storage, but it is equally consistent with retrieval-based reconstruction, which the authors acknowledge in passing but then dismiss without adequate justification.
issues.quote: the increase in memory illusions over time suggests that, in our experiments, participants mainly start out with a correct percept, which they quite accurately report when probed early after the memory display has disappeared. Over time illusions become more prevalent, indicating that correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter.

issues.subcategory: Cue color manipulation not validated — null result is uninterpretable
issues.description: Experiment 2 tested whether 'transiently induced expectations' (operationalized via fixation cross color predicting target type probability) could drive STM illusions. The post-experiment questionnaire confirmed participants did not report noticing the color-target contingency. The conclusion drawn is that 'expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.' However, because the manipulation was not verified as effective — participants showed no evidence of having learned the contingency, implicitly or explicitly — the null result is uninterpretable. It is impossible to know whether transiently induced expectations were absent or simply not induced by the undetected cue. A proper test of whether transient expectations modulate STM illusions would require verifying that expectations were actually induced (e.g., via an independent learning check, reaction time validation, or explicit training on the contingency). Without this, the conclusion about transient versus long-term expectations is unwarranted.
issues.quote: Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses... This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.

issues.subcategory: Misapplication of Fuzzy Trace Theory's similarity-inhibition prediction
issues.description: The authors argue that FTT is inconsistent with their data, citing FTT's prediction that 'high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should inhibit false memories.' This is a misapplication of FTT. Within FTT, the similarity-inhibition principle applies specifically to the relationship between studied items and critical lures in terms of their conceptual/semantic gist: semantically distinct critical lures are more susceptible to false recognition than highly similar ones because the gist of a semantically distant lure matches the stored gist. This principle was developed in the context of the DRM paradigm and refers to semantic/conceptual similarity among words or concepts. The mirrored letter Ɔ and C are not semantically similar in the FTT sense — they share the same semantic/lexical identity (the letter 'C') but differ only in their visual/physical orientation. Applying the FTT similarity-inhibition prediction to physical visual mirror symmetry constitutes a category error. The dismissal of FTT based on this misapplication is therefore invalid.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should inhibit false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant. Therefore, it seems that FTT cannot accurately account for the occurrence of this type of memory illusions in STM.

issues.subcategory: High exclusion rate in Experiment 2 with inadequate analysis of excluded participants
issues.description: In Experiment 2, 92 of 290 participants (31.7%) were excluded because they had 10 or fewer high-confidence trials in at least one cell of the design. The difference in mean high-confidence rates between included (49.2%) and excluded (15.7%) participants is substantial, representing a more than three-fold difference. This non-random exclusion means the published analysis reflects only participants who systematically respond with higher confidence — a sub-population that may differ on theoretically relevant dimensions (e.g., more categorical thinking, lower metacognitive sensitivity, stronger prior expectations). No sensitivity analysis using all participants, no examination of whether excluded participants show directionally consistent or opposite results, and no formal test of whether the exclusion criterion biases effect estimates are reported. With a 31.7% exclusion rate, selection bias is a serious concern for the validity of the reported findings.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions. Included participants had on average 49.2% high confidence trial over all conditions (range: 24.6 – 95.8, sd: 13.3). Excluded participants had on average 15.7% high confidence trials over all conditions (range 0.4 – 38.8%, sd: 9.5).

issues.subcategory: Short delay interval differs across experiments without justification
issues.description: The short memory delay condition is 750ms (probe at 0.75 seconds after memory display offset) in Experiments 1 and 2, but 500ms in Experiment 4. This inconsistency is never noted in the manuscript, yet it matters for interpreting the cross-experiment pattern of results and for the claim in the General Discussion that findings 'consistently' show illusions appearing within approximately 0.5–1 second. The theoretical argument depends on demonstrating that illusions arise 'when the memory display has only just disappeared' and the difference between 500ms and 750ms is not trivial given the rapid changes in memory fidelity claimed to occur within this timeframe. If the short delay is truly when the perceptual trace is 'intact,' then systematically varying this interval across experiments without comment makes cross-experiment comparisons difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: Each trial started with the presentation of a fixation cross on an otherwise blank screen for 0.5 seconds. After this, the memory display was presented for 0.25 seconds, a blank screen, only containing the fixation cross was presented for 0.5 (the Short condition) or 3 seconds (the Long condition).

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration for Experiments 1 and 2; stopping rules underspecified for Experiments 3 and 4
issues.description: Experiments 1 and 2 contain no mention of pre-registration, and multiple analytic decisions appear to have been made post-hoc or at least without documentation of a priori specification: the choice of exclusion threshold (10 trials), the specific ANOVA model structure, the decision to collapse across cue colors in Experiment 2 after observing a null effect, and the choice of which Bayes Factor threshold marks 'support' for each hypothesis. Experiments 3 and 4 use a sequential Bayesian stopping rule (continuing until BF > 10), which is described only briefly: 'Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.' The specification is incomplete: it does not state the prior distribution used, whether a specific Bayes Factor formulation (e.g., JZS prior, effect size prior) was committed to in advance, or how the testing schedule was chosen. Sequential analysis without complete pre-specification introduces flexibility in when and how to stop data collection.
issues.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets. Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent reporting of pseudo-letter illusion rates between Results and Discussion sections in Experiment 1
issues.description: The Results section of Experiment 1 states: 'For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase 12% as memory deteriorates through interference of time or visual information (29% illusions to 41% illusions).' The Discussion of Experiment 1 then states: 'the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from 29% to 39% and 43%, respectively' for the Long and Short-with-Interference conditions. The 41% in Results is the average of 39% and 43%, but this averaging is never explained. A reader of the Results section has no way to know that the 41% represents two distinct conditions with notably different rates (39% vs. 43%). Presenting an average of two conditions as if it were a single data point obscures the condition-level data and prevents evaluation of whether interference and delay have equivalent effects, which is theoretically relevant since they implicate different mechanisms of memory decay.
issues.quote: For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase 12% as memory deteriorates through interference of time or visual information (29% illusions to 41% illusions)... the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from 29% to 39% and 43%, respectively.

issues.subcategory: General Discussion illusion rate claim inconsistent with experiment-specific figures
issues.description: The General Discussion states: 'illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2) and up to 30% of reports when memory is probed at 3 seconds (Experiment 1-4).' However, Experiment 1 reported pseudo-letter target illusion rates of 29% at short delay and 39–43% at longer delays or with interference. These are substantially above 20% and 30%. The 20% and 30% figures appear to be averaged across target types and experiments, but this averaging is not explained and produces summary statistics that misrepresent the effect sizes actually observed. A reader relying only on the General Discussion would substantially underestimate the magnitude of pseudo-to-real illusions, which in some conditions approached 43% — a rate the authors themselves describe as 'almost as prevalent as correct responses.'
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2) and up to 30% of reports when memory is probed at 3 seconds (Experiment 1-4).

issues.subcategory: Cue color analysis scope in Experiment 2 not specified
issues.description: The analysis of cue color effects in Experiment 2 is described as analysing 'the illusory error rates (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) in an ANOVA with target type and cue colour as factors,' but does not specify whether this analysis was restricted to high-confidence trials (as in all subsequent analyses) or included all trials. This matters because the study's entire framework distinguishes high-confidence errors ('memory illusions') from low-confidence errors ('guesses'). If the cue color analysis included all confidence levels, it tests a different construct than the main analyses and cannot directly speak to whether transiently induced expectations modulate memory illusions specifically. The ambiguity makes the null result for cue color difficult to interpret and compare with the main analyses.
issues.quote: First, we tested whether the cue colour influenced the occurrence of illusory errors, analysing the illusory error rates (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter) and cue colour (red or blue, indicating low and high probability of a pseudoletter target) as factors.

issues.subcategory: No effect size estimates reported across any experiment
issues.description: No effect size estimates (e.g., partial η², Cohen's d, odds ratios, or posterior means with credible intervals) are reported for any comparison across all four experiments. Bayes Factors quantify evidence for or against an effect but do not convey effect magnitude. This is particularly problematic for a study making practical claims about the prevalence and magnitude of STM illusions in everyday cognition. For example, the claim that pseudo-to-real illusions are 'much more prevalent' than real-to-pseudo illusions is supported by large BFs but the reader cannot assess whether the absolute difference is 2 percentage points or 20. Without effect sizes, the practical and theoretical significance of the observed phenomena cannot be evaluated, and meta-analytic integration with future studies is substantially hampered.
issues.quote: The interaction between Target Type and Error Type (BFincl >1000) provides evidence for Hypothesis 3: when the target is a pseudo-letter, illusions are very common (37%) but other errors occur much less often (11%). For real letter targets, the illusory error rate is the same as the rate of erroneously selecting any other item from the response display (11% in both cases).

issues.subcategory: WEIRD student sample with domain-specific stimuli limits generalizability
issues.description: Experiments 2–4 recruited exclusively first-year psychology students at the University of Amsterdam, participating for course credit as part of their curriculum. This creates a doubly restricted sample: (1) Western, educated, industrialized, rich, democratic (WEIRD) demographics, and (2) a captive student population whose motivation to perform carefully may differ from volunteer participants. Furthermore, the entire paradigm depends on highly overlearned familiarity with the Latin alphabet, which is explicitly cited as the mechanism: 'participants have been exposed to the standard alphabet frequently and from a young age.' This means the effect is fundamentally dependent on a specific literacy background. The manuscript makes broad theoretical claims about 'STM in general,' 'the formation and maintenance of memory,' and the 'cognitive processing sequence for sensory input,' but these generalizations are not supported by a sample that could demonstrate cross-cultural, cross-literacy, or cross-age validity. No limitations related to sample characteristics are discussed.
issues.quote: These experiments specifically focus on a subset of false memories, namely what we call 'memory illusions'... All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet. Previous experience with letters should have provided participants with abundant evidence that letters typically appear in their standard form.

issues.subcategory: Interference and delay conditions conflated as equivalent in testing Hypothesis 2
issues.description: The key evidence for Hypothesis 2 ('illusions are memory-driven, not perceptual') rests on demonstrating that illusion rates increase over time. In Experiment 1, three conditions are used: Short (0.75s delay, no interference), Long (3s delay, no interference), and Short-with-interference (0.75s delay, plus an intervening visual display). The manuscript treats the Long and Short-with-interference conditions as equivalent demonstrations that 'memory deteriorates,' averaging over them in some analyses. However, these conditions represent mechanistically distinct forms of memory disruption: time-based decay versus proactive/retroactive interference from a new visual stimulus. The interference condition, which involves presenting a new letter display, could additionally disrupt the report phase rather than the retention phase, or introduce a response bias (since participants must evaluate two letter displays in one trial). Conflating these conditions as equivalent instances of 'memory deterioration' obscures whether the two mechanisms produce equivalent effects and prevents testing whether the specific mechanism of memory disruption matters for the development of illusions.
issues.quote: The Short with Interference condition (panel B) was the same as the Short condition, except that now the second letter display appeared together with the cue... the increase in illusory errors (7% increase from 19% in the short delay to 26% averaged over the short with interference and long delay) is larger than other errors (4% increase, from 8 to 12%).

issues.subcategory: Confidence rating used to distinguish illusions from guesses without validating calibration
issues.description: The entire analytical strategy hinges on the claim that high-confidence errors represent genuine 'memory illusions' (where participants have access to an incorrect memory trace) while low-confidence errors represent guesses or best-guesses. The authors argue that a response bias would predict stronger effects in low-confidence trials. While plausible, this assumes that confidence is well-calibrated and that participants can reliably introspect on whether their memory is genuine versus a guess. There is substantial evidence that confidence and accuracy are poorly dissociated, and that response biases — particularly those based on category-level priors — can systematically inflate confidence in biased responses. A participant who has no memory of the stimulus but knows that 'letters are usually real' may respond 'C' with high confidence precisely because of the prior, not because they have an illusory memory. The authors do not validate their confidence-as-illusion operationalization against any independent criterion, nor do they rule out that the 'high confidence' criterion simply selects trials where the prior expectation is particularly strong, regardless of memory quality.
issues.quote: Illusory memories should result in high confidence erroneous responses, where the participants has access to a memory trace (albeit an incorrect memory trace). In the absence of confidence ratings, the erroneous responses could actually consist of low confidence responses or even outright guesses.

issues.subcategory: Typographic error in Bayes Factor label
issues.description: In the Experiment 2 Results section, the text contains a typographic error in the Bayes Factor label: 'BFinlc>1000' should be 'BFincl>1000.' While minor, this introduces ambiguity in a manuscript where distinguishing between BFm (model Bayes Factor) and BFincl (inclusion Bayes Factor) is critical for correct interpretation of the statistical evidence. Readers unfamiliar with JASP output could misinterpret which statistic is being reported.
issues.quote: Participants were more likely to select the mirrored (pseudo) counterpart of a target than to commit other types of errors (18% vs 11%, main effect of error type, BFinlc>1000)

issues.subcategory: Reinterpretation of published findings without re-analyzing original data
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly argues that prior published studies (De Gardelle et al., 2009; Chalk et al., 2010) that interpreted their results as 'perceptual illusions' may instead reflect 'memory illusions,' because those studies only probed perception after stimulus offset. While this is a legitimate conceptual point, the authors then state these alternative interpretations as likely or plausible explanations, saying the current research shows the memory interpretation 'could also be' and is 'perhaps a more likely explanation.' However, neither De Gardelle et al.'s nor Chalk et al.'s original data are re-analyzed to test this claim, and no direct experimental comparison is conducted between a perceptual-probe and memory-probe version of those paradigms. The causal attribution of those published effects to memory processes rather than perceptual processes remains entirely speculative and goes beyond what can be concluded from the current experimental design.
issues.quote: However, the current research shows that this effect could also be due to a memory illusion: Perceivers might have seen the actual pseudo-letter, but just moments later remembered seeing the real letter. Moreover, Experiments 1, 2 and 4 show that this is perhaps a more likely explanation than an illusion that occurs when perceiving or encoding the stimuli.
